_readme: IPP-1731/1732: 6 extra Node.js Q&A with "Asked at" companies. Admin -> Bulk upload (dry run first). Only adds these questions; the language and other questions stay as they are.

questions.question: What happens from the moment a browser sends an HTTP request until your Express route sends the response?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The browser finds the server (DNS), opens a TCP connection (plus a TLS handshake for HTTPS) and sends the request. Node's http server parses it and hands it to Express, which runs your middleware in order, matches a route, runs the handler, and the handler writes the response back on the same connection.

How it works:
DNS: the domain becomes an IP address
TCP + TLS: a connection is opened and encrypted (HTTPS)
Node http server: parses the method, URL, headers and body stream, then emits "request"
Express: runs app.use() middleware in order (cors, express.json, auth, validation)
Route handler: does the work (database, other services) without blocking the event loop
Response: res.json() sets headers and the body; the connection stays open (keep-alive) for the next request

Example: POST /api/auth/login: cors() adds headers, express.json() parses the body, a rate limiter counts the attempt, validation checks the email, the controller finds the user in MongoDB, compares the password and returns a JWT with res.json().

Common mistake: A handler that neither sends a response nor calls next(err). The request hangs until the client times out.

Interview tip: Mention where things can go wrong at each step (DNS, TLS, CORS, a slow query) and how you would debug them with the browser Network tab and server logs.

questions.question: What is the difference between REST and gRPC, and when would you use each?
questions.answer:
Short answer: REST exposes resources over plain HTTP, usually with JSON, so any client (including browsers) can call it and people can read it. gRPC calls remote functions defined in a .proto file, sends binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2, and generates typed clients; it is faster and supports streaming, but browsers need a gRPC-Web proxy.

How it works:
Contract: REST is often documented with OpenAPI; gRPC has a required .proto file
Format: REST sends JSON text; gRPC sends compact binary messages
Transport: gRPC needs HTTP/2 and supports streaming in both directions
Tooling: REST works with curl and the browser; gRPC needs generated clients or special tools
Typical use: REST for public and browser-facing APIs, gRPC for internal service-to-service calls

Example: A MERN app's React frontend calls the Express REST API. Inside the backend, the order service calls the payment service with gRPC because it is fast and strictly typed.

Common mistake: Saying gRPC "replaces" REST everywhere. For a normal web app with a browser client, REST (or GraphQL) is simpler.

Interview tip: Mention the cost of switching: a .proto contract, code generation and harder debugging, which pays off only with many internal services.

questions.question: What is a message broker like Kafka or RabbitMQ, and when does a Node.js API need one?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A message broker sits between services: producers publish messages and consumers process them later, at their own speed. It decouples services, absorbs traffic spikes and allows retries. Kafka is a durable, replayable log built for very high throughput; RabbitMQ is a classic queue with flexible routing and per-message acknowledgements.

How it works:
Producer: the API publishes an event like "order.created" and responds to the user at once
Broker: stores the message safely until someone reads it
Consumer: a worker sends the email, updates stock or generates a PDF
Kafka: messages stay in a log for days, many consumer groups can read and replay them
RabbitMQ: a message goes to a queue and is removed after a consumer acknowledges it

Example: On checkout the API saves the order and publishes "order.created". The email, inventory and analytics services each consume it separately, so a slow email server never slows the checkout.

Common mistake: Adding Kafka to a small app. A simple job queue such as BullMQ on Redis is enough until you have many services or huge volume.

Interview tip: Talk about failure handling: retries, dead-letter queues and making consumers idempotent because a message can arrive twice.

questions.question: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS, and what does TLS protect?
questions.answer:
Short answer: HTTPS is HTTP sent through an encrypted TLS connection. TLS encrypts the data, proves the server's identity with a certificate, and detects any change to the data on the way. Plain HTTP sends everything, including passwords and cookies, as readable text.

How it works:
Encryption: nobody on the Wi-Fi or the network path can read the request or response
Authentication: the certificate, signed by a trusted authority, proves you are talking to the real domain
Integrity: a changed byte breaks the check, so data cannot be modified silently
Handshake: client and server agree on keys first (asymmetric), then use fast symmetric encryption
Default ports: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443

Example: A user logs in on public café Wi-Fi. With HTTP, anyone sniffing the network sees the password; with HTTPS they see only encrypted bytes and the domain name.

Common mistake: Thinking HTTPS hides everything. The domain (SNI) and IP address are still visible, and HTTPS does not protect against bugs like SQL or NoSQL injection.

Interview tip: Mention the practical side: Render and Vercel give free certificates, set secure cookies, and add HSTS so browsers always use HTTPS.

questions.question: Design a feature that shows how many visitors are online on a website right now.
questions.answer:
Short answer: First define "online", for example "seen in the last 60 seconds". Each open page sends a small heartbeat (or keeps a WebSocket open). The server stores each visitor's last-seen time in a Redis sorted set, counts the entries newer than 60 seconds, removes older ones, and pushes or serves that count to the pages.

How it works:
Visitor id: a random id in localStorage (or the user id when logged in), so one person with many tabs counts once
Heartbeat: every 20-30 seconds, or use the WebSocket connection itself
Store: ZADD online <now> <visitorId> in Redis; it is fast and shared by all Node instances
Count: ZCOUNT online <now-60s> +inf, and clean up with ZREMRANGEBYSCORE online -inf <now-60s>
Show: broadcast the count over WebSocket/SSE every few seconds, or let pages poll a cached endpoint
Scale: never write every heartbeat to MongoDB; Redis handles it, and the number can be slightly approximate

Example: A news site has three Node servers behind a load balancer. All of them write heartbeats to the same Redis sorted set, and one timer broadcasts "1,245 people reading now" every 5 seconds.

Common mistake: Counting open sockets on a single server (wrong with many servers), or never removing visitors who closed the tab.

Interview tip: Start with the questions an interviewer expects: exact or approximate? per page or whole site? how many users? Then size the design to the answers.

questions.question: Design a scalable REST API for a social media app with millions of users.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Start with clear resources and endpoints, keep the API servers stateless behind a load balancer, add caching and good indexes, use cursor pagination, move slow work to queues, and protect it with rate limits. Then explain how the feed is built, because that is the hardest part.

How it works:
Resources: /users, /posts, /posts/:id/comments, /users/:id/followers, /feed
Stateless servers: JWT auth, no sessions in memory, so you can add servers behind a load balancer
Pagination: cursor based (?after=<lastId>&limit=20), never skip/offset on huge collections
Database: indexes for every main query; shard or partition big collections like posts by user id
Caching: Redis for hot data (profiles, counters), a CDN for images and videos
Feed: fan-out on write (push post ids into followers' feeds) for normal users, fan-out on read for celebrities with millions of followers
Async work: a queue for notifications, image resizing and search indexing
Safety: rate limits per user and IP, idempotency keys for POSTs that may be retried

Example: GET /api/feed?after=abc&limit=20 reads 20 post ids from the user's Redis feed list, loads the posts in one query and returns nextCursor for the next page.

Common mistake: Jumping into a database choice before asking about scale and read/write patterns, or using offset pagination that gets slower on every page.

Interview tip: Ask about numbers first (daily users, reads vs writes), state the trade-offs (consistency vs speed for likes and counters), and draw the request flow.
